It's difficult to give advice like this, because I don't want to stomp out anything unique in your writing that might become something great later on, but I'll just give one example. Mind you, this is a very subjective sort of critique.  > Langden continued to tread down the road, until he came across a bridge.  Immediately, you give us a character and sense of space. Awesome. > He could only see because of the frequent lamp posts evenly spread on the path. A common alternative would be to imply that the reader is already knows we're viewing this scene from your protagonist's perspective. This makes "He could only see" a bit redundant, unless there is something specifically unique about your character's sense of sight. Often times once the reader is in your protagonist's point of view, you can just go on with descriptions and assume your reader will know who it's coming from. If you used, "Lanterns, evenly spaced, were the only road's source of light." We would know Langen is seeing this. He's the only character in the scene so far!  An alternative is to move the pronoun to add superior mental imagery. Here's a couple lines from the intro of a fantasy novel: "Wax peeked up over the knotted boards, scanning the empty town. **Blue lines hovered in his vision,** extending from his chest to point at nearby sources of metal, a result of his magic." He doesn't say, "He could see blue lines..." Instead he turns the visuals into the subject.  I don't think there's anything wrong about pronoun subject use, in fact many authors do that exact thing in the first paragraph, but the repetitious use of it can wear your reader out.

That lens is great. It's like old faithful for me. Great for some quick draw street photography on a sunny day.

On a typical zoom lens your "sweet spot" will usually be neither at the widest focal length, nor the lowest aperture. It really depends on the individual lens though. You can take some tests and figure it out.  I usually shoot with a prime lens and it's only slightly softer wide-open; the lens is so good that there's not much of a difference. With my zoom lens things begin to look look really good around f/5.6.

You're right, I'll just have to invest more time into testing these lenses out. I'm saving up for a big trip next year, which is why flipping the older gear is so tempting. The other lens is also faster, so I might end up using it at night anyways. (If only I had money for that specific wide-angle!) The lens in question is a very good lens for its price. I take mostly urban/street photography though, and rarely 'proper' portraits, so  I often find myself on the wider end of things. If you shoot crop-sensor like me, you could always grab a cheap telephoto. It's cheap and sharp, and I know a lot of people shoot portraits with longer focal lengths at f/4. I guess it all depends on your needs. I'd go crazy if I had to swap lenses every time I wanted to go wider than 28mm though!
I have a camera with fortunately has an articulated screen. Time to take lots of test footage.

Honestly my prime lens is so sharp there's no perceptible difference from f/2.8 and up. And, yeah, usually some area in the middle will look sharpest. An expert has a chart available online. Ultimately the only way you can know for sure is by testing the lens yourself, since there is always going to be variation. There's also user skill... tucking your elbow against your torso to gain stability, holding the camera well with both hands, etc. It sounds like a no-brainer but it took me months of practice just to hold the camera properly in a natural way.

I was detained in a foreign country after someone accused me of insulting a leader. The accuser was a local at a tourist site who ran scams on naive tourists. Earlier that day I had interfered with his racket, preventing a confused traveler from handing over local currency.  I returned to my accommodation at 9:00 p.m. and found him and his friends waiting outside. We shouted back and forth a few times. I ended up in police custody.  The police held me for 8 hours. They interrogated me slowly in bad English, and at random intervals burst out with "DID YOU INSULT THE LEADER?!" I told them I didn't. Then they transferred me to the real police station. I was to stay there for an indeterminate period of time, until a local official had a chance to meet me and decide my legal fate. Which was probably not good, since I remained silent half the time. But the local government cares little for my home country's laws. Fortunately I was released around 4 in the morning after a high-ranking officer strolled in, shrugged his shoulders, and told them to let me go. The cop who arrested me gave me a snack and drove me to the center of the sleeping town as a dust-storm rolled in. The story goes on from there, and there were a lot of details I left out. I plan on writing a book about my experiences one day.
